German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani speak during a ceremony for the signing of bilateral agreements in Berlin, Germany [Liesa Johannssen/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026
Qatar’s Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani has held talks with German leaders in Berlin on expanding defence and diplomatic cooperation, broadening a relationship long focused on trade and investment.
At a joint news conference with the emir on Friday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Qatar had pledged an additional 15 billion euros ($16.5bn) in investment, while the two governments planned closer cooperation on security and technology.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3What has happened to the $18bn pledged to Trump’s Board of Peace for Gaza?list 2 of 3US official says Hormuz insurance hits $64m: Is the strait really open?list 3 of 3Kuwait, Bahrain face new Iran attacks after US strike on Qeshm Islandend of list
Merz said the investment would strengthen cooperation in artificial intelligence (AI), computer chips and aviation. He also expressed Germany’s interest in developing defence industry partnerships with Qatar, while the two countries agreed to work together to improve protection against cyberattacks.
The discussions come as Qatar continues pushing for a diplomatic solution to end the US-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a major route for global oil and gas supplies.
Sheikh Tamim also held talks with German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, who proposed a regional security conference for the Middle East.

The United States Senate has passed a bipartisan bill to speed up approvals for power plants, transmission lines and other energy projects as lawmakers face pressure to bring down electricity bills and meet growing demand fuelled by the growth of artificial intelligence.
The Senate voted 62-33 on Thursday as 15 Democrats, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, backed the bill and two Republicans voted against it.

President Donald Trump had urged senators to pass the measure and said he would sign the bill if it passes the House of Representatives.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would shorten timelines for federal reviews for energy projects and limit how approvals may be challenged in court.
It would change several environmental laws, including the National Environmental Policy Act, which requires federal agencies to weigh a project’s environmental effects and gives the public a chance to weigh in before a project is approved.
The four senators who coauthored the bill, two from each party, argued that Americans are tired of paying high utility bills while projects that could lower them are stuck in the planning phase.

Santiago Abascal, wearing a blue suit and tie, looks straight into the camera. His campaign poster makes three promises: giving Spanish nationals priority in access to benefits, cutting regulation and “remigration”.

Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3How will Spain’s housing crisis affect elections?list 2 of 3Spain pushes to suspend TikTok after probe into child sex abuse videoslist 3 of 3EU prosecutor office investigates fatal train crash in Spainend of list
With little more than a week to go until Spain’s November 29 snap election, opinion polls put Vox in third place behind the conservative Popular Party (PP), which is leading the race, and the governing Socialist Party.
But with the Socialists’ potential allies fragmented and the PP projected to fall short of an outright majority, Vox could emerge as a kingmaker.
The party, which once struggled to win a single seat in parliament, could join a PP-led coalition or back a minority PP government from outside the cabinet.
What is Vox, and who founded it?
Abascal was a regional lawmaker for the PP in the Basque Country. He left the party in 2013, accusing then-Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy of being too soft on the issue of Catalan separatism. He went on to cofound Vox.
The new party positioned itself to the PP’s right, making Spanish unity its central cause. It called for an end to the country’s system of regional autonomy and championed the idea of the “true Spaniard”, who was Catholic, Castilian-speaking and loyal to the monarchy.

Tommee Sherwood poses with flowers after arriving in Algiers [Courtesy of Taylor Mah/City of Lawrence, Kansas]By Madjid SerrahPublished On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026
Algiers, Algeria – Tommee Sherwood never expected that Algeria would come to play such a big role in his life.
Until recently, the 70-year-old from Lawrence, Kansas – a retired university custodian, musician, and volunteer English teacher for refugees – had never been to North Africa before and knew Algeria mostly from the film The Battle of Algiers.
He was aware, though, that Algeria had given refuge to members of the Black Panther Party in the 1970s, including Pete O’Neal, chairman of the Kansas City chapter.
“That connection between Algerians and Kansas City goes way further than most people realise,” he told Al Jazeera.
Sherwood was among 38 residents of Lawrence who visited Algeria from November 9-15 at the government’s expense as a gesture of gratitude from President Abdelmadjid Tebboune for the way their small university city had welcomed the Algerian national team, which used Lawrence as their official base camp during the World Cup.
Five months on, the football was long over, but the genuine bond it had forged between two communities separated by 8,000km (5,000 miles) had only grown stronger.
On a boat in the Bay of Algiers on their first day in the country, a DJ was playing.
“He started playing some old jazz music,” Sherwood recalls in audio messages sent to Al Jazeera. “And he was playing some old timers – some old Kansas City guys that I used to know. It really touched me.”
He gave the DJ a small gift and took photographs. The next day, the same DJ was playing at a different event. He came over to Sherwood and handed him three vintage 45s – old recordings of Algerian singers. Advertisement

Poland has said Russia violated its airspace three times overnight, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said was a “provocation” by Moscow.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz told a news conference on Friday that investigations were under way at three locations – Nowy Lipowiec, roughly 60km (37 miles) from the Poland-Ukraine border, Molodycz, about 50km (31 miles) to the south, and Rudnik nad Sanem, about 50km to the west.

The incursions were reported as Poland held military exercises involving the “Coalition of the Willing“, a group of European countries coordinating help and support for Ukraine.

item.title: Blood Gold: The Munduruku’s fight for survival in the Brazilian Amazon
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration 25 minutes 00 seconds play-arrow
25:00
Fault Lines investigates how illegal gold mining poisons and threatens Indigenous communities in the Brazilian Amazon.Read more
For the Munduruku people of the Brazilian Amazon, the fish they depend on for survival have become poisoned with mercury. As soaring gold prices drive illegal miners deeper into the rainforest, mercury used to extract the gold contaminates rivers and enters the food chain, putting entire communities at risk.
In Blood Gold, Fault Lines meets Indigenous families confronting the health consequences of illegal mining and fighting to protect their land. With rare access to an illegal mine, senior correspondent Josh Rushing witnesses how mercury is used to extract gold. He meets a researcher documenting the contamination of Indigenous communities and a federal prosecutor working to stop the mercury trade. The film examines why illegal mining persists despite government crackdowns and who pays the price for the world’s appetite for gold.Published On 20 Nov 202620 Nov 2026

A potato war is cooking in Japan.
For the first time in 76 years, the country may be forced to lift a ban on United States potato imports under intense pressure from President Donald Trump.

The proposal, which has not been confirmed yet, is already prompting strong opposition from Japanese potato farmers who said the move could expose their crops to harmful foreign pests and diseases from imported batches. They also said cheap imports would impact their own sales.
The US first requested that Japan lift its import ban in 2020 during Trump’s first term. Now Washington has turned up the heat. In March, lawmakers urged Trump to discuss the matter during a planned meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.
Tokyo has begun seriously considering the matter – possibly to use as a bargaining chip during Trump’s trade and tariff wars, observers said.
The issue was discussed again when Japanese officials visited Washington, DC, in September. Now, Japan’s Ministry of Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries is moving forward by first identifying potential problems, including diseases and pests, and then seeking measures from the US to avoid them, Japanese media reported.
